sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Scleroderma citrinum forms a firm, sometimes flattened ball about 2–12 cm across, without a distinct stem and attached to the ground by mycelial cords. Its thick, ochre-yellow skin bears coarse brown scales or warts, sometimes arranged in rosettes around a central pyramidal point.

sections.title: Cut surface and maturation
sections.text: The gleba is pale and firm at first, then mottled grey-purple and white before turning violet-black. At maturity the interior becomes dark and powdery, and the outer skin splits irregularly. The microscopic spores are round and strongly ornamented.

sections.title: Habitat
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal fungus grows on the ground near broad-leaved or coniferous trees, sometimes among woody debris, in woods and parks. It appears mainly from late summer into autumn.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: A young edible puffball is generally white and uniform inside, while Scleroderma has a thick leathery skin and gleba that darkens early. This comparison is not sufficient to establish edibility. The genus Scleroderma has been implicated in poisonings; French records from 2000–2022 cover the whole genus and were not all identified to species. Do not eat it.

traits: Irregular ball, often flattened at the poles, 2 to 12 cm, almost no stem, fixed to the ground by mycelial cords
Very thick skin (1 to 5 mm), ochre yellow with brown scales, cracking into pyramidal warts
Dense inside, pale grey at first, then violet-black marbled with white, powdery at the end
Tough outer skin 1–5 mm thick, with brown warts often arranged in rosettes
The gleba changes from pale to grey-purple marbling and then violet-black; it becomes powdery and the skin splits irregularly at maturity
Ectomycorrhizal near broad-leaved or coniferous trees · late summer to autumn
safetyNote: Do not eat: the genus Scleroderma is toxic and has been implicated in digestive poisonings. French records from 2000–2022 include several species and do not support attributing every reported symptom to S. citrinum.
